 Texas early voting for 2026 could break record
 BY 
 Lauren Rangel
 Texas 
 PUBLISHED 5:30 PM CT Oct. 27, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 5:30 PM CDT Oct. 27, 2026 
 SHARE 
 TEXAS — There’s one week left before the midterm elections, and Texas is seeing flocks of early voters at the polls before the big night.
 In Ellis County, which sits just to the south of Dallas, a steady stream of people went in and out of a local polling station.
 “No problems. Got into the voting machine, no problems. Everything went pretty smooth in there,” said Solomon Redmond, a voter.
 He is one of the nearly 5 million early voters so far.
 “I had to vote. It’s pretty ugly out there,” said Redmond.
 Texas is currently on track to beat the 2022 midterm turnout of 5.51 million voters. That was also a non-presidential election year.
 “What’s coming out is kind of expected for this midterm election,” said Jana Onyon, Ellis County election administrator. “We always plan kind of at least getting up to the amount that comes out in a presidential, but we never see it.”
 Onyon said the county has 360 poll workers this time around. That’s fully staffed in her book.
 “We’re looking really well for staffing and making sure our polling locations are ready to go,” said Onyon.
 There are 30,000 newly registered voters in Ellis County this year, and it’s a trend that’s felt statewide, according to political consultant Derek Ryan.
 “We've seen voter registration increase every two years for decades now,” said Ryan.
 With the growing number of voters, more people are voting early, too.
 “There's been a real shift in people voting early versus voting on Election Day, and I think in this election, we could see a possibility of 80% of all votes being cast during early voting,” said Ryan.
 Despite the uptick in registered voters, people in Ellis County said voting lines moved quickly this week.
 “About 15 minutes,” said Redmond.
 “It wasn’t even a wait in there. Just a walk through,” said Shanetia Hill, a voter.
 Spectrum News wanted to know how long people would be willing to wait, so we asked voters.
 “Oh, I would wait all day if I had to,” said Brad Wrzesinski, a voter.
 But the consensus on a reasonable amount of time for most: “Fifteen to 20 minutes is reasonable,” said Wrzesinski.
 Most counties allow residents to see polling site wait times online. For Dallas, that website is linked here. 
 Onyon added that they also recruit students 16 and older to help through the local high schools. They have about 100 students this year. It’s something students can do all over the state and get paid for.
